newsitem.title: INDIA: Rosy Indian economy masks disturbing trends.
newsitem.headline: Rosy Indian economy masks disturbing trends.

text.p: Slackening industrial growth, mounting inflation, lacklustre exports -- India's economy shows worrisome signs which analysts said the government will be hard pressed to address in its budget blueprint next week.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, who on February 28 will present the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year which starts on April 1, will have some evidence to paint a sunny picture of current economic conditions.
The government estimates gross domestic product (GDP) will expand by 6.8 percent in 1996/97, yielding a respectable average annual growth rate of seven percent over the past three years.
The current account deficit is expected to be no more than 1.5 percent of GDP -- under 1.6 percent in 1995/96 and well below the 2.0 percent level which the central bank thinks safe.

Chidambaram is expected to announce that the closely watched fiscal deficit will drop to as low as 5.1 percent of GDP from 5.9 percent in 1995/96, analysts said. His target for 1997/98 is believed to be about 4.5 percent.
Foreign exchange reserves stood at a healthy $24 billion last month, up from $21 billion a year earlier, and the rupee has been broadly stable since an abrupt depreciation last year.

"The external situation is pretty solid and not cause for current concern," said an international banker close to the government's reform programme. "But the economic indicators may be telling something more disturbing for the future."
GDP growth in 1996/97 will be largely due to a one-off, four-percent jump in agricultural output.

Manufacturing growth is forecast to slow to 10.6 percent from 13.6 percent in 1995/96. Growth in production in five core infrastructure sectors -- electricity, coal, steel, petroleum and cement -- dipped to 3.3 percent in April-November 1996 from 9.3 percent in the same period in 1995.
"I don't think growth will reach 7 percent in 1997/98," said Ashok Desai, the finance ministry's former chief adviser.
"We are finding now that seven percent growth is unsustainable," said an analyst with an international bank. "We may be looking at an underlying growth rate of six percent."

Desai attributed the anticipated growth slowdown to over-investment in 1993/94 and stringent monetary policy. "Nothing in the budget stimulates growth. It is all consumption," he said, citing costly, ill-targeted subsidies.

Bankers said many firms were holding back on investments, partly because of mixed signals from Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left coalition government. "Companies are hitting infrastructure bottlenecks," one banker said.
Analysts said wide-open debate within the government between free traders and nationalists had confused investors, who were looking for hurdles to infrastructure investment to be lifted.
"Investors are tired of hearing reforms are irreversible," a banker said. "They want concrete results on the ground."
Desai said: "The government has an unduly unfavourable image among foreign investors. It is reformist but does not convince."
Weak exports and rising inflation are particularly worrisome, analysts said.

Exports, which have shown double-digit growth in recent years, rose by 6.4 percent in April-December 1996 over the same period in 1995. Exports may fall some $5 billion short of the $38 billion goal for 1996/97, Business Standard newspaper said.
The annual inflation rate measured by the wholesale price index rose to 7.73 percent in the week ending February 1 from 4.68 percent one year earlier.

Desai predicted the rate would top 10 percent by mid-1997. Real interest rates will remain high unless the government presses ahead more aggressively with a lacklustre programme to sell partial stakes in state firms, analysts said.

"Chidambaram is a lot more friendly to inflation than his predecessor," Desai said, referring to Manmohan Singh, who spearheaded reforms from 1991 to last May. "He won't mention inflation at all. He will give a naively optimistic picture and say anyone who is complaining is just whining."
